query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a dense, well-adherent CrN coating on boride-based components will significantly improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components with a native, uncoated surface.
generation.intervention: Sputter deposition of a dense CrN coating on the boride surfaces.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at typical plating temperatures (e.g., 700–750 °C) for prolonged durations in a hot-dip aluminum-plating process.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous CrN layer forms a diffusion barrier, preventing direct chemical interaction between molten aluminum and the underlying boride substrate.
generation.mechanism: The CrN coating inhibits aluminum penetration by limiting ion diffusion and suppressing the formation of deleterious reaction products (such as aluminum-boride compounds), thereby reducing corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated boride components, the CrN-coated components will exhibit a significantly lower rate of corrosion, evidenced by reduced weight loss and diminished surface degradation after molten-aluminum exposure.
generation.baseline: The performance of boride components without the CrN coating under identical molten-aluminum exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: The protective effect of the CrN coating is expected to remain effective so long as the coating maintains its integrity and adhesion; extreme thermal cycling, mechanical damage, or temperatures that exceed the coating’s stability limit could compromise performance.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum coating thickness, exact deposition parameters, and long-term behavior of the CrN layer under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical boride-based components: one set with a sputter-deposited CrN coating and one uncoated control group. Subject both sets to molten aluminum immersion at temperatures typical of hot-dip aluminum-plating for a fixed duration. Post exposure, assess corrosion using weight loss measurements, surface morphology analysis (e.g., SEM), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrN-coated components do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate and surface degradation compared to the uncoated controls, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: With the rapid development of high-temperature sectors such as the aerospace and power generation industries, the demand for metallic materials that maintain exceptional mechanical properties under high-temperature conditions has significantly increased. Recent studies have revealed that refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) based on refractory elements such as tungsten (W), molybdenum (Mo), niobium (Nb), and tantalum (Ta) exhibit superior high-temperature strength and good fatigue resistance, surpassing the currently used nickel-based superalloys [,]. However, RHEAs, such as the MoNbTaVW alloy [], typically have high densities and exhibit brittleness at room temperature, which limits their application scope. The addition of aluminum (Al), with its low density and large atomic radius, induces lattice distortions when forming solid solutions with refractory metals, reducing the system’s free energy, thereby enhancing solution strengthening effects. Therefore, Al is often added to RHEAs to reduce alloy density and improve specific strength. In addition, to obtain a uniform and stable protective layer, sputtering technology offers a fast deposition rate and a low-cost solution. Although the development of HEA systems has been going on for more than a decade, there are few reports on the deposition of stable protective films on HEA surfaces by conventional reactive sputtering techniques. Many studies have shown that sputter deposition of CrN film on conventional stainless steel is beneficial for its wear and corrosion resistance [,]. The CrN film deposited on the surface of 316 stainless steel has a positive effect on the friction behavior in NaCl solution and high temperature environments until heated to 550 °C []. In the tribo-corrosion test, the CrN coating layer can also remain relatively stable during the ball-on-plate sliding under various applied potentials []. As stainless steels are similar to CoCrNi-based MEAs in terms of their single FCC structure and lattice constant, this study attempts to sputter CrN film with a Cr buffer layer on the surface of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA and discusses in detail the improvement of corrosion and wear resistance of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA by sputtering CrN film.

reading.lever: Apply a dense, well-adherent CrN coating via sputter deposition on boride surfaces.
reading.why: This approach, proven on similar systems for high-temperature corrosion resistance, can create an effective barrier against molten aluminum attack on boride components.
